questions.question: What happens when you read from or write to a nil Go map?
questions.title: What happens when you read from or write to a nil Go map
questions.direct_answer: The zero value of a map is nil. Reading, deleting, ranging, and taking `len` are safe on a nil map, but assigning a key panics because no writable map storage has been initialized. `make(map[K]V)` or a map literal creates an initialized map. A nil map and an empty initialized map both have length zero, yet only the initialized one accepts writes.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
The zero value of a map is nil. Reading, deleting, ranging, and taking `len` are safe on a nil map, but assigning a key panics because no writable map storage has been initialized.

`make(map[K]V)` or a map literal creates an initialized map. A nil map and an empty initialized map both have length zero, yet only the initialized one accepts writes.

For example, `var counts map[string]int` allows `counts["go"]` and returns zero, but `counts["go"]++` panics. `counts := make(map[string]int)` makes the increment valid.

Map values are reference-like descriptors. Assignment shares the same map, and ordinary maps also need synchronization when goroutines read and write concurrently.

A nil map is safe as a read-only empty result or optional value when callers know that contract. Initialize it before any path that may add entries.

sections.title: The core model: nil and empty maps in Go
sections.content:
nil and empty maps in Go is easiest to understand by following the data or control from input to result. The details below form one connected model rather than a list of unrelated rules.

Safe reads make optional lookup convenient: the zero value and comma-ok result behave consistently even when the map itself is nil. Writing needs internal storage for buckets and metadata, so the runtime rejects assignment to a nil descriptor rather than silently allocating through a value the caller may not own.

nil and empty maps in Go at a glance
sections.content:
| Operation | Nil map | Empty initialized map |
|---|---|---|
| `len(m)` | 0 | 0 |
| `m[key]` | Zero value, false | Zero value, false |
| `range m` | No iterations | No iterations |
| `delete(m,key)` | Safe | Safe |
| `m[key]=value` | Panics | Works |

sections.title: The practical decision: nil and empty maps in Go
sections.content:
The useful question is not whether nil and empty maps in Go can be used, but which requirement makes it the clearest and safest fit. That decision includes its cost and its failure boundary.

Returning nil can avoid an allocation when absence and empty mean the same thing. APIs that promise a writable map or a particular JSON shape should return an initialized empty map instead. The contract matters more than choosing one form universally.

sections.content:
nil and empty maps in Go and an initialized empty map solve related problems, but they expose different guarantees. The best choice follows from the guarantee the program actually needs.
